## 1. US Crime Dataset

### 1.1 Load test dataset 'crimedata'

Data download from: https://github.com/mpjashby/crimedata

The goal of crimedata is to access police-recorded crime data from large US cities using the Crime Open Database (CODE), a service that provides these data in a convenient format for analysis. All the data are available to use for free as long as you acknowledge the source of the data.

The function returns a tidy data tibble or simple features (SF) object of crime data with each row representing a single crime. The data provided for each offense includes the offense type, approximate offense location and date/time. More fields are available for some records, depending on what data have been released by each city. For most cities, data are available from 2010 onward, with some available back to 2007. Use to see which years are available for which cities.get_crime_data()list_crime_data()

More detail about what data are available, how they were constructed and the meanings of the different categories can be found on the CODE project website. Further detail is available in the paper Studying Crime and Place with the Crime Open Database.

Data can be downloaded by year and by city. By default (i.e. if no arguments are specified, 'get_crime_data()') a 1% sample of data for all cities for the most recent available year is returned.

```{r}
#install.packages("crimedata")
library(crimedata)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
#help(crimedata)

# To get a sample of 1%. Time period from 2010 to 2017 
 crime <- get_crime_data(
   years = 2010:2017,
   cities = NULL,
   quiet = TRUE,
   output = 'sf'
 )
 
# Select variables 
crime_select <- select(crime, 'city_name', 'offense_type', 'offense_group', 'offense_against', 'date_single', 'geometry')

# Calculate the crime rate by offense_year, city and offense_type
crime.rate_select <- crime_select %>% 
  mutate(offense_year = year(date_single)) %>%
  group_by(offense_year,city_name,offense_type) %>%
  summarise(Incidents = n()) %>%
  mutate(pct = Incidents/sum(Incidents))
```

You can alternatively get a simple features (SF) point object with the correct co-ordinates and co-ordinate reference system (CRS) specified by setting the argument output = "sf". This can be used to quickly plot the data.
For example, to analyze personal robberies in the sample data:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
personal_robberies <- subset(crime, offense_type == "personal robbery")
subset(crime, offense_type == "personal robbery") %>%
  mutate(offense_year = year(date_single)) %>%
  ggplot()+
  geom_sf()+
  facet_wrap(vars(offense_year), nrow = 4)
```

```{r}
personal_robberies %>% 
  mutate(offense_year = year(date_single))%>%
  group_by(offense_year,city_name)%>%
  summarise(Incidents = n()) %>%
  mutate(pct = Incidents/sum(Incidents)) -> pr.rate
pr.rate <- pr.rate[!is.na(pr.rate$offense_year),]
```

### 1.2 Install package 'spGARCH'

The function 'qml.spARCH' fits a spatial ARCH model using the maximum-likelihood approach. In addition, external regressor may be included in the mean equation.

```{r setup}
install.packages("spGARCH")
library(spGARCH)
help(spGARCH)
```


### 1.3 Calculate weighing matrix W for the test data

'spdep' is a collection of functions to create spatial weights matrix objects.

```{r}
library(sf)
#install.packages("spdep")
library(spdep)
coords <- st_centroid(st_geometry(pr.rate), of_largest_polygon=TRUE,na.rm = TRUE)

# choose K nearest neighbours for spatial weights
col.knn <- knearneigh(coords, k=3)
st_geometry(pr.rate)
nblist <- knn2nb(col.knn)
W <- nb2mat(nblist)

```

### 1.4 Test the function with sample crime data. For example, use the US personal robberies.

```{r}

qml.robberies <- qml.spARCH( pct ~ city_name + offense_year, data = pr.rate, W = W)
qml.step <- step(qml.robberies)
summary(qml.step)

```

## 2. London Crime Dataset

### 2.1 Load test dataset 'London Crime'

Data download from Kaggle:
https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/jboysen/london-crime?resource=download

Context:
Crime in major metropolitan areas, such as London, occurs in distinct patterns. This data covers the number of criminal reports by month, LSOA borough, and major/minor category from Jan 2008-Dec 2016.

Content:
13M rows containing counts of criminal reports by month, LSOA borough, and major/minor category.

Acknowledgements:
Txt file was pulled from Google Cloud Platform and converted to csv. Photo by James Sutton.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(tidyverse)
london_crime <- read_csv("data/london_crime_by_lsoa.csv")

length(unique(london_crime$borough))
# 33 boroughs

london_crime.rate <- london_crime %>% 
  group_by(borough, year, major_category, minor_category) %>%
  summarise(Incidents = n()) %>%
  mutate(pct = Incidents/sum(Incidents))
```

Select one kind of crime and one year:
```{r}
pr.rate <- subset(london_crime.rate, minor_category == "Theft From Shops")
pr.rate <- subset(pr.rate, year == '2016')
```

### 2.2 Install package 'spGARCH'

```{r setup}
#install.packages("spGARCH")
library(spGARCH)
help(spGARCH)
```

### 2.3 Calculate weighting matrix 'W'

Besides, the geometry information is needed to calculate the weighting matrix 'W'. So the shape file for London boroughs is download from:
https://data.london.gov.uk/dataset/statistical-gis-boundary-files-london

```{r}
library(sf)
library(spdep)
london_map <- st_read(
  "london_shape/London_Borough_Excluding_MHW.shp")

#for (i in 1:9414) {
#  for (j in 1:33) {
#  ifelse(london_map[j,1] %in% london_crime.rate[i,1],
#    london_crime.rate[i,7] <- london_map[j,8], NA)
#  }
#}

london_crime.rate$geometry

london_map$NAME
str(london_map)

get_centroids <- function(x){
  borders <- NULL
  for(i in 1:length(london_map$geometry[[x]])){
    borders <- rbind(borders, london_map$geometry[[x]][[i]][[1]])  
  }
  return(apply(borders, 2, mean))
}

centroids <- t(sapply(1:33, get_centroids))

london_map$geometry[[14]][[2]]

# plot(london_map$geometry[[14]])
# points(centroids[14,1], centroids[14,2], col = "red")
plot(london_map$geometry)

# plot(london_map$geometry[[20]], add = TRUE, col = "red")
points(centroids[,1], centroids[,2], col = "red")

# choose K nearest neighbours for spatial weights
col.knn <- knearneigh(centroids, k = 3)
nblist <- knn2nb(col.knn)
W <- nb2mat(nblist)

nb_object <- poly2nb(london_map)
W <- nb2mat(nb_object, style = "W")

image(W)
apply(W, 1, sum)

```

### 2.4 Test the function with sample crime data: 'Theft from shops' at 2016

```{r}

qml.pr <- qml.spARCH( pct ~ borough, data = pr.rate, W = W)
qml.step <- step(qml.pr)
summary(qml.step)
```

### 2.5 Append some other possible factors to 'London Crime'

Download the Data set 'housing density':
https://data.london.gov.uk/dataset/land-area-and-population-density-ward-and-borough

Land area and population density figures for 2001 to 2050 for wards and boroughs. Ward data begins in 2011.
Population figure included are GLA estimate (2016-based projections), 2011 Census and ONS Mid-year Estimates.
GLA figures are based on GLA population projections. Select which year you require from the drop-down box in the spreadsheet.
Inland area takes account of water line. Areas with large bodies of water will have a smaller inland area than total area since some of the area will be water.
Land area figures are taken from Ordnance Survey boundaries using MapInfo.

```{r}
housing_density <- read_csv("housing-density-borough.csv")
#View(housing_density)

housing_density <- subset(housing_density,Year == 2016 & ! Name %in% c("London","Greater London","Inner London","Outer London"))
unique(housing_density$Name)
```
Append the population density to pr.rate. Test the model again
```{r}
colnames(housing_density)[2] = 'borough'
pr.rate <- merge(pr.rate, housing_density[c(2,10)] ,by = "borough", all = TRUE)
```

```{r}
qml.pr <- qml.spARCH( pct ~ borough + Population_per_square_kilometre, data = pr.rate, W = W)
qml.step <- step(qml.pr)
summary(qml.step)
```
